{{Short description|When formal languages generate the same set of strings}}{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}

In [[formal language]] theory, '''weak equivalence''' of two [[formal grammars|grammar]]s means they generate the same set of strings, i.e. that the formal language they generate is the same. In [[compiler theory]], where only [[context-free grammar]]s are considered, weak equivalence is distinguished from '''strong''' (or '''structural''') '''equivalence''', which additionally means that the two [[parse tree]]s are reasonably similar in that the same semantic interpretation can be assigned to both.<ref name="Reghizzi2009">{{cite book|author=Stefano Crespi Reghizzi|title=Formal Languages and Compilation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AxH6cWm61i0C&pg=PA57|year=2009|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-84882-049-4|page=57}}</ref>

Two grammar formalisims are '''weakly equivalent''' if they define the same set of string languages.{{cn|date=September 2026}} This notion is an instance of [[Weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence in homotopy theory]].{{cn|date=September 2026}}
Vijay-Shanker and Weir (1994)<ref name="vijayshankarAndWeir1995">{{cite journal | url=http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.52.4044&rep=rep1&type=pdf | author=Vijay-Shanker, K. and Weir, David J. | title=The Equivalence of Four Extensions of Context-Free Grammars | journal=Mathematical Systems Theory | volume=27 | number=6 | pages=511&ndash;546 | year=1994 | doi=10.1007/BF01191624 | s2cid=12336597 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> demonstrated that [[Indexed grammar|linear indexed grammar]]s, [[combinatory categorial grammar]]s, [[tree-adjoining grammar]]s, and [[head grammar]]s are weakly equivalent formalisms in that meaning.

On the other hand, if two grammars generate the same set of derivation trees (or more generally, the same set of abstract syntactic objects), then the two grammars are strongly equivalent. Chomsky (1963)<ref name="Chomsky.1963"/> introduces the notion of strong equivalence, and argues that only strong equivalence is relevant when comparing grammar formalisms. Kornai and Pullum (1990)<ref name="kornaiAndPullum1990">Kornai, A. and Pullum, G. K. 1990. ''The X-bar Theory of Phrase Structure''. Language, 66:24-50.</ref> and Miller (1994)<ref name="miller1994">Miller, Philip H. 1999. ''Strong Generative Capacity''. CSLI publications.</ref> offer a refined notion of strong equivalence that allows for isomorphic relationships between the syntactic analyses given by different formalisms. Yoshinaga, Miyao, and Tsujii (2002)<ref name="yoshinagaMiyaoAndTsujii2002">{{Cite web |url=http://www-tsujii.is.s.u-tokyo.ac.jp/~yoshinag/papers/yoshinag-tagplus6.pdf |title=Yoshinaga, N., Miyao Y., and Tsujii, J. 2002. ''A formal proof of strong equivalence for a grammar conversion from LTAG to HPSG-style''. In the Proceedings of the TAG+6 Workshop:187-192. Venice, Italy. |access-date=2012-02-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110828092423/http://www-tsujii.is.s.u-tokyo.ac.jp/~yoshinag/papers/yoshinag-tagplus6.pdf |archive-date=2011-08-28 |url-status=dead }}</ref> offers a proof that for any [[Tree-adjoining grammar|LTAG]] formalism, there is a strongly equivalent [[Head-driven phrase structure grammar|HPSG]] one.

==Context-free grammar example==
[[File:Parse Tree Derivations ETF.svg|300px|thumb|''Left:'' one of the parse trees of the string "1+2*3" with the first grammar. ''Right:'' the only parse tree of that string with the second grammar.]]
As an example, consider the following two [[context-free grammar]]s,<ref group=note>with the [[start symbol (formal languages)|start symbol]] "<nowiki><expression></nowiki>"</ref> given in [[Backus-Naur form]]:

<syntaxhighlight lang="bnf">
<expression> ::= <expression> "+" <expression> | <expression> "-" <expression>
               | <expression> "*" <expression> | <expression> "/" <expression> 
               | "x" | "y" | "z"   |   "1" | "2" | "3"   |   "(" <expression> ")"
</syntaxhighlight>

<syntaxhighlight lang="bnf">
<expression> ::= <term>   | <expression> "+" <term>   | <expression> "-" <term>
<term>       ::= <factor> |       <term> "*" <factor> |       <term> "/" <factor>
<factor>     ::= "x" | "y" | "z"   |   "1" | "2" | "3"   |   "(" <expression> ")"
</syntaxhighlight>

Both grammars generate the same set of strings, viz. the set of all arithmetical expressions that can be built from the variables "x", "y", "z", the constants "1", "2", "3", the operators "+", "-", "*", "/", and parentheses "(" and ")".
However, a [[concrete syntax tree]] of the second grammar always reflects the usual [[order of operations]], while a tree from the first grammar need not.

For the example string "1+2*3", the right part of the picture shows its unique parse tree with the second grammar;<ref group=note>using the abbreviation "E", "T", and "F" for <nowiki><expression></nowiki>, <nowiki><term></nowiki>, and <nowiki><factor></nowiki>, respectively</ref> evaluating this tree in [[postfix traversal|postfix order]] will yield the proper value, 7.
In contrast, the left picture part shows one of the parse trees for that string with the first grammar; evaluating it in postfix order will yield 9.

Since the second grammar cannot generate a tree corresponding to the left picture part, while the first grammar can, both grammars are not strongly equivalent.

==Generative capacity==
In linguistics, the '''weak generative capacity'''<!---in bold, since this term redirects here---> of a [[generative grammar|grammar]] is defined as the set of all strings generated by it,<ref group=note>for context-free grammars: see [[Context-free grammar#Context-free language]] for a formal definition</ref> while a grammar's '''strong generative capacity'''<!---in bold, since this term redirects here---> refers to the set of "structural descriptions"<ref group=note>for context-free grammars: [[concrete syntax tree]]s</ref> generated by it.<ref name="Bach.Miller.2003">{{cite book | contribution-url=http://www.kornai.com/MatLing/gencapfin.pdf | author1=Emmon Bach |author2= Philip Miller | contribution=Generative Capacity | doi=10.1093/acref/9780195139778.001.0001 | isbn=9780195139778 | editor=William J. Frawley | title=International Encyclopedia of Linguistics | publisher=Oxford University Press | edition=2nd | year=2003 }}</ref>
As a consequence, two grammars are considered weakly equivalent if their weak generative capacities coincide; similar for strong equivalence.
The notion of ''generative capacity'' was introduced by [[Noam Chomsky]] in 1963.<ref name="Chomsky.1963">{{cite book | author=Noam Chomsky | contribution=Formal properties of grammar | pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofmathem017893mbp/page/n334 323]&mdash;418 | editor1=R.D. Luce | editor2= R.R. Bush | editor3= E. Galanter | title=Handbook of Mathematical Psychology | location=New York | publisher=Wiley | volume=II | year=1963 |url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofmathem017893mbp }}</ref><ref name="Bach.Miller.2003"/>
